week-1.Meaning and Etymology of Sanatana Dharma: Even the term 'Sanatana Dharma' is not an official name for our religion but it is a term that means 'eternal dharma', because it is a dharma that always existed. It is important that we as Hindus understand the literal meaning of Sanatana Dharma. 'Sanatana' traces its roots as 'sada bhava', which, after Samskrita grammar treatments, becomes 'Sanatana'. 'Sanatana' means that which exists (bhava) always (sada); eternal, ever-present, permanent. 'Dharma' traces its root to the root verb 'dhr' meaning that which upholds, supports, or maintains everything. 'Dharma' can also mean 'an essential quality' or 'true innate nature' of an entity. Sanatana Dharma is that ever-present one that never ceases to be, the one which can never be destroyed; eternal, universal, Cosmic Law - the natural order and harmony which sustains life and the universe. On a personal level, it is that which, if we follow, will make us contented and happy - the path to realize lasting happiness by aligning one's thoughts, words, and acts with Universal Values as delineated by the Vedic scriptures (Shastras).
week-1.Origin of the Term Hinduism: 'Hinduism' is a name given to Sanatana Dharma by western researchers. Our religion originally had no name because, initially, it was the only one that existed. How did our religion then come to be called Hinduism? According to historians, every civilisation has grown along the banks of a river because people subsisted on agriculture and maintenance of cattle. History refers to the civilisation that existed along the banks of river Sindhu as the 'Indus Valley Civilisation', 'Indus' being a later variation of the name 'Sindhu'. The people who lived along the river Sindhu were at first called Sindhus. Over a period of time, the term morphed into Hindus, and thus the term Hinduism came about.
week-1.How Sanatana Dharma Differs from Other R: Is Sanatana Dharma 'a Religion' like we hear about other religions like Christianity, Judaism, Islam? Yes, for legal purposes to ensure rights of the practitioners are protected (Article 25 of the Indian Constitution). The differences are: 1. No 'one founder' or prophet. 2. No one rigid book (Sri Swamiji says, "Others may have a holy book; ours is a huge library!"). 3. Plural and inclusive. 4. Heavy emphasis on inquiry versus blind dogmas. 5. No one can clearly establish its 'start date'. 6. If at all we need to name a 'founder', Bhagavan himself is the founder of our Sanatana Dharma - that is why every tradition within our Dharma traces its origin in Bhagavan himself. Our Sanatana Dharma is as old and young as Existence itself.
week-1.The Vedas as the Supreme Pramana: The authoritative texts which establish the true knowledge of Dharma are called 'Pramanas'. (Prama means truth 'as it is'; that which establishes this is Pramana.) The primary pramana, the supreme authority, are the 'Vedas' (four branches). Apart from the Vedas, there are 10 more texts which expand or supplement the Vedas, making 14. Adding the four appendices, we have totally 18 first-level Pramanas. Vedas means 'Knowledge'. This is considered to be the divine knowledge of Bhagavan Himself and hence is the 'root' of all creation. They are truly 'infinite' - says the Vedas themselves. They are the 'life breath' of Bhagavan. Bhagavan said in Srimad Bhagavad Gita: "I am known through all the Vedas" (vedaishcha sarvai: ahameva vedya: - BG 15:15). The Rishi Apastamba said: "Vedas are the Pramana of all Dharma." The Vedas are not a product of human intelligence (Sanskrit term: Apaurusheya). The pronounced sound of the Vedas is the key - the sound itself has creative ability.
week-1.The Four Vedas - Rig, Yajur, Sama, Athar: If at all we need to point to one rishi in history as a rejuvenator of our Dharma, it is Sage Veda Vyasa, the divine incarnation of Bhagavan's 'Jnana', born to Sage Parashara and Satyavati Devi. Sage Veda Vyasa codified the Vedas into 4 branches: 1. Rig - 'Hymn in praise' (Riks). 2. Yajur - 'Worship with sacrifice'; ritualistic procedures. 3. Sama - means 'peace to minds'; Riks set to music. 4. Atharva - types of mantras to ward off evil and hardship, discovered by a Rishi named Atharvan.
week-1.The Four Portions of the Vedas: The Vedas have four main portions, likened to a tree: 1. Samhita - the 'collection' of mantras (divine chants); the trunk. 2. Brahmana - the Vedic rituals which use the mantras; the branch. 3. Aranyaka - the 'forest' portion, philosophy; the unripe fruit. 4. Upanishads - the 'conclusions' of the Vedas, the inner meaning and 'jnana' (knowledge) portion; the fruit.
week-1.The Two Itihasas - Ramayana and Mahabhar: There are 2 Itihasas and 18 Puranas in the canvas of Sanatana Dharma scriptures. The Itihasas (literally 'it verily happened thus') are: 1. Srimad Ramayanam - 24,000 slokas by Sri Valmiki Maharshi. 2. Sriman Mahabharatam - 100,000+ slokas by Sri Veda Vyasa Maharshi.
week-1.The 18 Puranas and Their Three Gunas: The 18 Puranas (literally 'ancient', but actually timeless) are traditionally grouped by the Gunas - the qualities of Satvika, Rajasa, and Tamasa. There are 18 Puranas in all, with about 400,000 verses combined. All 18 were written by Veda Vyasa, except the Vishnu Puranam (by Parashara). Satvika Puranas: Vishnu Purana, Narada Purana, Srimad Bhagavata Mahapurana, Garuda Purana, Padma Purana, Varaha Purana. Rajasa Puranas: Brahma Purana, Brahmanda Purana, Brahmavaivarta Purana, Markandeya Purana, Bhavishya Purana, Vamana Purana. Tamasa Puranas: Shiva Purana, Linga Purana, Skanda Purana, Agni Purana, Kurma Purana, Matsya Purana. The Srimad Bhagavata Mahapurana has 18,000 slokas and its primary focus is Krishna / Vishnu.
week-1.The Pramana Hierarchy - Vedas, Itihasas,: The hierarchy of pramanas, from highest authority to widest base, is Vedas, then Itihasas, then Puranas - shown as a pyramid with the Puranas as the widest base, the Itihasas in the middle, and the Vedas at the top. All of them harmoniously show the same or integral knowledge of Truth and Dharma. In case of apparent contradictions, the higher authority takes precedence.

week-2.The Prasthana Traya: The journey through our Sanatana Dharma's philosophy rests on three main pillars: 1. Upanishads, 2. Bhagavad Gita, 3. Brahma Sutras. Together, these three are referred to as the 'Prasthana Traya'. Prasthana means journey; Traya is a 'set of three'. Hence Prasthana Traya means the essential three for Sanatana Dharma's philosophical journey. It can be pictured as a temple whose roof is Sanatana Dharma, resting on these three pillars. These three pillars form the foundation of Vedanta - the quest for the Supreme Truth. Pillar 1, the Upanishads, comes from the Vedas; Pillar 2, the Bhagavad Gita, comes from the Itihasas; Pillar 3, the Brahma Sutras, was composed by Sage Veda Vyasa.
week-2.Pillar 1 - The Upanishads and the Dasopa: Pillar 1 is the Upanishads. The Upanishads are the very 'fruit' of the Vedas. A tree's ultimate purpose for humanity is generally its fruit, so the Upanishads hold an important place in the Vedas. We have about 108 mainstream Upanishads from all four branches of the Vedas (Rig, Yajur, Sama, Atharva). Of these, 10 occupy a prime spot. The number 10 in Samskritam is called 'dasa', so the 10 Upanishads are the 'Dasa-Upanishads' or 'Dasopanishads': 1. Isha, 2. Kena, 3. Katha, 4. Prashna, 5. Mundaka, 6. Mandukya, 7. Taittiriya, 8. Aitareya, 9. Chandogya, 10. Brihadaranyaka. The Upanishads are the primary authority or source of religious knowledge on the highest truth or 'tatva-gnana' (philosophy), and form the first pillar for almost all denominations within our Sanatana Dharma.
week-2.Pillar 2 - Srimad Bhagavad Gita: Pillar 2 comes from the middle of the pyramid, the Itihasas. This is none other than Srimad Bhagavad Gita, the divine discourse between Bhagavan and Sri Arjuna in the Mahabharata. The Mahabharata is a huge Itihasa with 18 sections named parvas: the first is the Adi Parva ('first section') and the last (18th) is the Swarga-arohana Parva ('Ascent to Heaven' section). Srimad Bhagavad Gita is in the 6th section, the Bhishma Parva, chapters 25-42. Some details: total verses (slokas) - 700; chapters (adhyayas) - 18; number of names of Bhagavan mentioned - 18 (e.g. Hrshikesha, Krishna, Achyuta); slokas that Bhagavan Sri Krishna graces - 574; slokas Arjuna speaks - 84; slokas Sanjaya speaks - 41; slokas Dhritarashtra says - 1. It integrates the paths of Karma Yoga, Raja Yoga, Bhakti Yoga and Gnana Yoga into a unitary whole.
week-2.Pillar 3 - The Brahma Sutras: Pillar 3 is the Brahma Sutras. Sage Veda Vyasa gave a synthesis of all the Upanishads, harmonising them to show that the message cutting across all Upanishads is one and the same without any real conflict. He gave this in the form of aphorisms (sutras - short, distilled, concise rules). The Brahma Sutras are organised as: 4 chapters (called Adhyaya), 16 sections (called Padam; 4 padams make an Adhyaya), many topics (called Adhikarana), and many aphorisms (called Sutras; one or more Sutras make an Adhikarana). The number of sutras varies by tradition: Advaita has 555 sutras and 223 topics; Vishishtadvaita (Sri Vaishnava) has 544-545 sutras and 156 topics; Dvaita (Sri Madhvacharya) has 564 sutras and 223 topics. The second sutra is "Janmadyasya yatha:", which is also the opening phrase of the Srimad Bhagavata Mahapurana.
week-2.Srimad Bhagavatam as the Essence of the: Srimad Bhagavatam covers all three foundational pillars by being the essence, expansion, and purport of all three. For the Upanishads pillar (from the Garuda Purana verse: gayatri-bhashya-rupo'sau vedartha-paribrimhitah), Srimad Bhagavatam is a detailed commentary on the Gayatri mantra and is the very essence of all the Upanishads. Sage Veda Vyasa also says 'puranam brahma sammitam' (SB 1.3.40), meaning Srimad Bhagavatam is to be seen with the same reverence as the Vedas themselves - it is equivalent to the Vedas. And 'nigama kalpa taror galitam phalam' (SB 1.1.3) - it is the fruit and essence of all the Vedas, in a form accessible to one and all.

For the Bhagavad Gita pillar (from the Garuda Purana verse: bharatartha-vinirnayah), Srimad Bhagavatam is the essence of Sage Vyasa's Mahabharata, and Srimad Bhagavatam is graced by the very author of the Mahabharata - Sage Veda Vyasa himself.

For the Brahma Sutras pillar (from the Garuda Purana verse: artho'yam brahma-sutranam), Srimad Bhagavatam is the true meaning and commentary of the Brahma Sutras, graced by its very author Sage Veda Vyasa himself. For example, the first shloka of Srimad Bhagavatam expounds on the second Brahma Sutra. Srimad Bhagavatam is also called the 'sama roopa' of the Puranas - the essence and harmonised form of all the Puranas.
week-2.Srimad Bhagavatam Is Bhagavan Himself: Shastras usually show the way to attain Bhagavan. As Srimad Bhagavatam is the essence of all shastras, it not only shows how to attain Bhagavan, but what makes it unique is that Srimad Bhagavatam is Bhagavan Himself. This is outlined in the Padma Purana. Thus Srimad Bhagavatam is the avatara of Bhagavan Sri Krishna in the form of words. It is said that the words of Srimad Bhagavatam are Sri Radha Devi and the meaning is Sri Krishna Himself. The Padma Purana describes the greatness of Srimad Bhagavatam in six chapters (the Srimad Bhagavata Mahatmyam); the 3rd chapter of that Mahatmyam details a conversation between Sri Krishna and Uddhava. As Krishna is about to return to Vaikunta, Uddhava asks Him not to go, in order to protect His devotees from Kali Yuga, and Krishna says that He shall remain on Earth in the form of Srimad Bhagavatam. This is what Sri Swamiji sings in his composition, "Srimad Bhagavatam Svayam Harireva" - Srimad Bhagavatam is Bhagavan Himself.

week-3.The Three Levels of a Purana Story - Dha: A Purana story can be embellished in three deeper levels: a) Dharma - righteousness, the do's and don'ts, the underlying value; b) Tattva - the underlying philosophical principle or tenet; c) Rasa - the relish or aesthetic flavour expressed poetically. Great ones generally tell stories to all; dharma to a thousand; tattva to ten; and rasa to one. Srimad Bhagavatam is a rare Purana that is almost exclusively for Rasikas. Let us be a Rasika by divine grace, to relish this journey the most.
week-3.The Four Major Puranas on Srimad Bhagava: Four major Puranas speak extensively about the greatness (Mahatmya) of Srimad Bhagavatam: the Skanda Purana, the Padma Purana, the Garuda Purana, and the Naradiya Purana. The Skanda Purana extols the glory of holy pilgrimage places (tirtha); the Padma Purana celebrates the greatness of religious vows (vrathas); the Garuda Purana explains the importance of shraddha (ancestral rites); and the Naradiya Purana highlights the power of mantras. All of them proclaim at length the Srimad Bhagavata Mahatmya to demonstrate that, in the age of Kali, Bhagavata Dharma is the true refuge. On the other hand, Srimad Bhagavatam does not talk about the greatness of any other Purana, as it shines independently.
week-3.Srimad Bhagavatam as the Essence of Othe: Srimad Bhagavatam is the essence of all shastras, canto by canto: the 1st Canto is the Mahabharata's essence; the 9th Canto is the Ramayana's essence; the 4th Canto is the essence of Shiva bhakti; the 11th Canto is Srimad Bhagavad Gita's essence; and the 7th Canto is the essence of all Smritis and Dharma shastras.
week-3.The Parikshith and Nectar Episode: The Parikshith and Nectar episode: When Shuka Maharishi took his seat in the assembly of sages to give Srimad Bhagavatam to Parikshith Maharaja, the Devas arrived there with a bowl of amruta (nectar). They prostrated to Shuka Maharishi and prayed, "Let Parikshith have this bowl of nectar, and we shall have the nectar of Srimad Bhagavata." Shuka Maharishi merely laughed, thinking, "This amruta of the Devas is incomparable to Srimad Bhagavata amruta. This is like comparing a piece of glass to a precious gem." Knowing this, and that the Devas were not devotees, Shuka Maharishi did not give them the nectar in the form of Srimad Bhagavatam. Purport (Tattva): the word amruta can mean the tasty divine drink in Devaloka, or 'a-mruta' - conquering death, signifying moksha. This episode is narrated at the very outset to clarify that Deva amruta is nowhere close in comparison to Srimad Bhagavata amruta.
week-3.The Brahmaji and the Measuring Episode: The Brahmaji and the Measuring episode: Brahmaji was stunned to witness Parikshith's emancipation as a result of listening to Srimad Bhagavatam. In Satyaloka he set up a weighing balance and placed all the divine scriptures on one side and Srimad Bhagavatam on the other. The plate with all the other scriptures weighed less, and the side with Srimad Bhagavatam proved to be superior. All the Rishis who witnessed this regarded Srimad Bhagavatam as Bhagavan Himself and capable of granting speedy access to Srivaikuntha when read or listened to. Purport: Sri Brahmaji is the very embodiment of our Vedas and hence the greatest impartial pramana for us. A means is greater than others if it is either the easiest, or a sure way to attain the same goal. Srimad Bhagavatam is not only the easiest and a sure-shot way to attain Bhagavan, but it excels all because it is the end itself - being verily Sri Bhagavan Himself.
week-3.Narada's Encounter with Bhakti Devi: The Narada Maharishi and Bhakti Devi episode: The four Kumaras (Sanaka, Sanandana, Sanatana, Sanatkumara), the mind-born sons of Brahma, arrived in Badarikashrama and met Sage Narada, who looked very dejected. Narada described visiting Earth and seeing the effects of Kali Yuga everywhere - no truth, kindness, compassion, devotion, or selflessness. On the banks of the river Yamuna he saw a distressed young woman beside two unconscious old men, being fanned by hundreds of women. She said, "I am Bhakti Devi. These two are my children, Jnana and Vairagya. These ladies are the holy rivers in living forms." She said: "I was born in Dravida and matured in Karnataka. I was celebrated here and there in Maharashtra and attained a ripe age in Gujarat. Afflicted by Kali Yuga I too lost my splendor along with my sons. I became young again after reaching Brindavana." Narada told her that her renewed youth was due to her contact with Holy Brindavan, and that her sons remained old because they are neglected by everyone. He tried to awaken Jnana and Vairagya by chanting the Upanishads and the Bhagavad Gita, but they only rose slightly and fell back into sleep. A celestial voice then said that Narada must perform a 'satkarma' (a righteous act), which saints would point out to him.
week-3.The Prescription of the Srimad Bhagavata: The four Kumaras told Sage Narada that the satkarma is the jnana yagna of the reading of the Srimad Bhagavata Mahapurana: "By the chanting of Srimad Bhagavatam, bhakti, jnana, and vairagya shall gain strength. All the evils of Kali Yuga shall disappear." Narada asked how Jnana and Vairagya could be awakened by Srimad Bhagavatam when the Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita could not, since Srimad Bhagavatam is itself the essence of the Vedas. The Kumaras replied: just as the essence of a tree can be enjoyed only in the form of the fruit; just as ghee in milk cannot be tasted, but the same ghee separated from the milk gives joy even to Devas; just as sugar permeates the entire sugarcane yet tastes sweeter when separated - Srimad Bhagavatam, though the essence of the Vedas, also has an existence apart from them and serves as the fruit. Where should it be done? At the holy place of 'Ananda' on the banks of the river Ganga near Haridwar. How many days? Srimad Bhagavatam should be read every day, but considering the age of Kali, a reading of the complete text in 7 days has been prescribed. The full procedure is detailed in the 6th chapter of the Srimad Bhagavata Mahatmyam found in the Padma Purana. When the hall was full, the Kumaras told Bhakti Devi and her sons to take a seat in the hearts of all those listening to Srimad Bhagavatam.
week-3.The Atma Deva and Dhundhukari Story: The Atmadeva and Dhundhukari episode is one of the four stories told by Veda Vyasa Bhagavan to reveal the greatness of Srimad Bhagavatam. Dhundhukari, who lived a sinful life and returned as a ghost after his death, is liberated when Gokarna recites Srimad Bhagavatam over seven days for his sake. The purport is that regardless of one's past, a person can be fully purified and liberated simply by hearing Srimad Bhagavatam.

week-4.The Story of Atmadeva: The Story of Atmadeva: 1. Atmadeva and his wife Dhunduli had everything except a child. A great sanyasi gave them a divine fruit, but fearing pregnancy Dhunduli secretly fed it to their cow instead. 2. The cow bore a divine child, Gokarna, with cow-like ears. Dhunduli's sister's baby, Dhundhukari, was passed off as her own; he grew to be wicked and cruel while Gokarna grew wise and devoted. 3. Grieved by Dhundhukari's ways, Atmadeva renounced the world and attained the Lord's feet by reading the 10th canto of Srimad Bhagavatam, on the advice of Gokarna. Dhundhukari wasted his life in sin and, when his money ran out, was burned to death, becoming a ghost tormented by hunger and thirst. 4. Gokarna arranged a saptaha (seven-day recitation) of Srimad Bhagavatam for Dhundhukari's sake. The ghost entered a hollow bamboo with seven nodes to listen to the divine katha, one node bursting open each evening. 5. By the seventh day all the nodes had opened; Dhundhukari was freed from his sins, attained a divine form, and went to the Lord's abode, followed by Gokarna. Purport: even a person as sinful as Dhundhukari - a thief, a cruel man who spent his life in bad company - could be completely purified and bestowed liberation, simply through sincerely listening to Srimad Bhagavatam for seven days. Even sacred rites like shraddha performed at holy places were not enough to free him. From the most spiritual Gokarna at one end of the spectrum to the most sinful Dhundhukari at the other, and Atmadeva in the middle, all are uplifted by this great Purana.
week-4.The Effects of Srimad Bhagavatam (Mahatm: In a nutshell, Srimad Bhagavatam: a) dispels the fear of samsara - the cycle of birth and death - naturally; b) enhances devotion in the heart, effortlessly; c) increases Krishna's love towards us, steadily; d) purifies the mind thoroughly, painlessly; e) is the result of heaps of past punya. All this is because Srimad Bhagavatam is the essence, sum and substance of all scriptures; it was revealed by Sage Veda Vyasa as the last Purana - his final work, and so covered all his earlier words; and Srimad Bhagavatam is Krishna Himself. Just as Vittala came from Dwarakadeesha and is Krishna Himself as archavatara, likewise Srimad Bhagavatam came from the lotus lips of Vasudeva and is Sri Vasudeva Himself.
week-4.The First Lineage of Transmission: The four stories detailing the Srimad Bhagavata Mahatmyam in the Padma Purana were a result of the discussion at Naimisharanyam (known today as Nimsar) between Shaunaka rishi and Ugrashravas Suta. The divine lineage of Srimad Bhagavatam's transmission is: 1. Sri Vasudeva, 2. Sri Brahmaji, 3. Sri Narada Maharishi, 4. Sri Veda Vyasa Maharishi, 5. Sri Shuka Muni, 6. Parikshit Maharaja and Ugrashravas Suta, 7. Shaunaka Rishi. Veda Vyasa Bhagavan added all the events of 1 to 7, plus three more introduction shlokas, giving us Srimad Bhagavatam in the form we see today. In this first lineage, Sri Shuka Muni transmits it two ways: to Parikshith Maharaj, and to Ugrashravas Suta, who transmits it to the Shaunaka Rishi(s). The transmission from Narada Maharishi to Sage Veda Vyasa is the divine bridge between this world and the worlds above, through the medium of 'yoga dasa', and this bridge is the reason for the lineage's effective divinity and eternity.
week-4.The Second Lineage of Transmission: The Second Lineage of Transmission and the content of the divine knowledge transmitted through it are covered in Srimad Bhagavatam cantos 3 and 4. The second lineage runs: Bhagavan Vasudeva to Sri Shankarshana to Sanatkumara to Sankhyayana Rishi, who transmits it two ways - to Brihaspathi (Devaguru), who transmits it to Uddhava Swami; and to Parashara Muni, who transmits it to Maithreya Rishi, who transmits it to Vidura.
week-4.Structure of Srimad Bhagavatam: The structure of Srimad Bhagavatam: the total number of Cantos (skandhas) is 12; the total number of Chapters (adhyayas) is 335; the total number of Verses (shlokas) is 18,000. The numbering code 1.2.23 means 1st Canto, 2nd Chapter, 23rd Verse. Purana means 'ancient' - sacred literature presenting the abstract concepts of the Vedas in an understandable form through examples and stories. Mahatmyam is the glory of a scripture, told through stories that reveal its unique greatness.
week-4.Speakers and Listeners of Srimad Bhagava: The prime speakers of Srimad Bhagavatam, in order, are Sage Veda Vyasa, Ugrashravas Suta, Sri Shuka Muni, and Sage Maithreya. The listeners are Vidura, Raja Parikshith, the Shaunaka Rishi(s), and 'us' - today's readers and listeners.

week-5.The Three Types of Samhitas: Three types of Samhitas: 1. The Vedas are known as 'Raja Samhita'. The Vedas issue commands - they do not coax or plead with us; they command us like a king, saying, "Speak the truth; remain steadfast in dharma." 2. The Puranas are known as 'Suhrt Samhita'. The word suhrt means 'friend'. The Puranas explain spiritual truths to us in a friendly, kind, and approachable manner. Srimad Bhagavatam is a sattvika Purana; it never threatens or intimidates, but presents the very same truths taught by the Vedas in a delightful and appealing manner. 3. Certain other sacred compositions are known as 'Kanta Samhita' - divinely inspired works of great poetic beauty. Just as a loving wife speaks gently, gracefully, and appropriately to her husband, the Kanta Samhita conveys spiritual truths with tenderness and charm. Sri Swamiji's Madhurageethams are Kanta Samhitas.
week-5.The Five Classical Lakshanas of a Purana: 'Purana' literally means 'ancient'. It is sacred literature, a compilation of stories from ancient history, which presents the abstract concepts of the Vedas in an easily understandable form through examples and stories. According to the Matsya Purana, five specific lakshanas (characteristics or subjects) need to be present for a scripture to qualify as a Purana: 1. Sarga - primary creation of the 'principles of the universe' by Bhagavan; 2. Pratisarga - secondary creation of the universe by Brahma; 3. Vamsha - genealogies of devas, rishis, and kings; 4. Manvantara - the periods of rule of the various Manus; 5. Vamshanucharita - dynastic history (the solar and lunar dynasties).
week-5.Srimad Bhagavatam as a Maha-Purana with: Srimad Bhagavatam is unique - it is called a 'Maha'-Purana. It has 10 lakshanas, five more than other Puranas; these are delineated in canto 2, chapter 10 of Srimad Bhagavatam. So are all ten the principal subjects of the scripture? No. 'Ashraya' is the sole principal (main) subject. The other nine are there only to direct us towards Ashraya - to purify us so that we can fully realize this subject. Ashraya is Sri Krishna, the Brahman.
week-5.The Twelve Cantos and Their Dominant Lak: Each canto of Srimad Bhagavatam covers a dominant lakshana (characteristic or subject), though each may also carry fragments of other lakshanas. There are 12 cantos and only 10 lakshanas. The dominant lakshana of each canto is: Canto 1 - Preface (the greatness of the listeners and speakers); Canto 2 - Introduction of the name of the text, table of contents and a summary; Canto 3 - Sarga (primary creation of principles); Canto 4 - Visarga (secondary creation of 8.4 million types of living organisms); Canto 5 - Sthanam (sustenance by Bhagavan's will); Canto 6 - Poshanam (Bhagavan's grace on devotees); Canto 7 - Uthi(s) (latent impressions or vasanas); Canto 8 - Manvantara (the reign of the various Manus); Canto 9 - Ishanukatha (stories of the solar and lunar dynasties, of Bhagavan, and of bhagavatas' lives); Canto 10 - Ashraya (Krishna katha); Canto 11 - Mukti (liberation from the cycles of birth); Canto 12 - Nirodha (souls withdrawing into Bhagavan during dissolution).
week-5.Canto 1 as the Adhikari Skandha: Canto 1 serves as an introduction to Srimad Bhagavatam. It shows the greatness of the expounders and listeners of Srimad Bhagavatam: Narada Maharishi (chapters 5, 6); Sri Veda Vyasa Bhagavan (chapters 4, 5); Sri Shuka muni (chapters 2, 4); Sri Parikshith Maharaj and his ancestors (chapters 7-19); Sri Ugrashravas Suta / Suta Pauranika (chapter 1); and the Shaunaka Rishi(s). Some mahans hence call it the 'Adhikari Skandha' - the skandha that speaks of the apt and fit person to listen to and expound this grand Purana, in order to derive the fruit of associating with the text.
week-5.Outline of Canto 1: Outline of Canto 1: the 6 questions of the Shaunaka Rishi(s) to Suta Pauranika (chapter 1); Suta Pauranika's answers to the questions (chapters 2-3); the discussion between Sage Vedavyasa and Sage Narada (chapters 4-6); glimpses of Parikshith's great ancestors - Arjuna, Draupadi, Uttara, Kunti, Yudhishthira, Bheeshma (chapters 7-9); Sri Krishna returns to Dwaraka (chapters 10-11); the birth of Parikshith (chapter 12); all the ancestors ascend to higher worlds (chapters 13-15); Parikshith subdues Kali (chapters 16-17); and Parikshith's curse and fortune (chapters 18-19).
week-5.Highlights of Canto 1 - Stutis and Prala: Highlights of Canto 1, which has 19 chapters and 809 verses. Two main Stutis (praises): 1. Kunti Stuti (8th chapter, 26 verses); 2. Bheeshma Stuti (9th chapter, 11 verses). Two minor Stutis: 1. the Women of Hastinapura (10th chapter, 10 verses); 2. the People of Dwaraka (11th chapter, 4 verses). Two Pralapas (divine laments): 1. Arjuna's to Dharmaputra (15th chapter, 23 verses); 2. Mother Earth's to Dharma Devata (16th chapter, 11 verses). The canto starts with six questions by Shaunaka Rishi in the first chapter and ends with six questions by Raja Parikshith in the last chapter, showing the earnestness of the listeners.
week-5.The Six Questions of Shaunaka Rishi: In the sacred land of Naimisharanya, a great congregation of sages led by Sri Shaunaka Rishi assembled and undertook a sacrifice (yagna) spanning a thousand years to please Bhagavan. In the intervals between their rituals, Sri Suta Pauranika was engaged to discourse on the Puranas. The Shaunaka Rishi(s) asked him six questions: 1. What is the ultimate good for the people in this Kali Yuga? Answer: Hari Bhakti, devotion to Lord Hari. 2. Why did Bhagavan descend as the son of Devaki and Vasudeva? Answer: to nourish devotion. 3. Please describe the Gambheera leela of Bhagavan (His leela of creation, sustenance and dissolution of the universe). Answer: discussed in Cantos 2 and 3. 4. Describe all his incarnations. Answer: Varaha - Canto 3; Matsya and Kurma - Canto 8; Narasimha - Canto 7; Vamana - Canto 8; Parasurama and Sri Rama - Canto 9; Balarama and Sri Krishna - Canto 10; Kalki - Canto 12. 5. Describe the leelas Bhagavan did along with Balarama. Answer: described in detail in 90 chapters of Canto 10. 6. Where did Dharma take refuge after Bhagavan's leela samvarana (departure)? Answer: in the age of Kali, Dharma has sought refuge in the Divine Names of the Lord.

week-6.Suta Pauranika on True Dharma and Devoti: Sri Suta Pauranika was thrilled to have been chosen by the eminent sages for this service. After paying respects to Sri Shuka, Sri Vyasa, Lord Narayana, Nara and Devi Saraswati, he lauded the questions put forth by the sages. That practice of supreme dharma alone which gives rise to devotion in our hearts to Hari - characterized by an intense longing to listen to the stories of Sri Krishna - is the path to attaining the highest good; practices of dharma that do not lead to such devotion are ultimately in vain. The mundane outlook on life runs: Dharma to Artha (wealth) to Kama (pleasure) to enjoyment of the senses, and back to more Dharma. The blissful revolutionary path shown by Srimad Bhagavatam runs: Artha to Dharma to Bhakti to Jnana to Ananda. This Supreme Reality can be attained through Bhakti alone; Satsanga, the association of holy devotees, awakens the desire for devotion. Sri Veda Vyasa taught this Purana to his son Sri Shuka, who in turn related it to King Parikshith, who was seated on the banks of the Ganga with a vow to fast unto death (prayopavesha).
week-6.Shaunaka Rishi's Four Further Questions: In chapter 4, Sri Shaunaka Rishi asked Suta Pauranika to expand on four points: 1. When, where, and why this discourse was held. 2. Who inspired Sri Veda Vyasa to compose this Purana. 3. How Sri Shuka, who was an enlightened soul, came to learn this Purana from his father. 4. Why King Parikshith quit his kingdom and took a vow to fast unto death, and how he got to meet Sri Shuka and listen to the Purana from him.
week-6.Sage Vyasa's Birth and Restlessness: Suta Pauranika started the story from the avatara of Sri Veda Vyasa. In the Dwapara Yuga, Sage Vyasa was born to Satyavati and Sage Parashara. Seated in meditation in his ashram on the banks of the River Saraswati, Sage Vyasa saw the sufferings of all in Kali Yuga and worried for their welfare. Feeling dissatisfied with all his works thus far - the composition and compilation of the other Puranas, the Mahabharata, and so on - he wondered what else he could do to help the people of Kali Yuga, and felt restless.
week-6.Sage Narada's Arrival and Advice to Vyas: In chapters 5 and 6, Sage Narada arrived at Sri Vyasa's ashram and was duly worshipped and welcomed by Sage Vyasa. When Sage Vyasa asked Sage Narada to discern why he was feeling restless, Sage Narada pointed out that he still needed to compose a scripture describing the glories and leelas of Bhagavan - none of the works he had authored so far were dedicated to extolling them. Sage Narada then told the story of his own past birth, to inspire Sage Vyasa to compose a scripture which would in turn inspire devotion to Bhagavan in the hearts of its listeners.
week-6.Narada's Previous Birth - Sadhus and Cha: Narada Maharishi's story: in his previous birth, born as the son of a maid in a village, Sage Narada was blessed with the company of sadhus who had camped in his village during the four months of the rainy season, having undertaken the chaturmasya vratha. Being in their constant company, his ears were filled with the glories of Bhagavan, which they discussed incessantly. While leaving the village at the end of the rainy season, they instructed this child on the highest truth.
week-6.Narada's Previous Birth - Vision, Divine: Shortly after, Sage Narada's mother passed away, bitten by a snake. Seeing the hand and grace of Bhagavan even in adversity, the child left the village and walked towards the north. Finding a place of solitude, he sat to meditate on the Lord as taught by the sadhus. Though by their grace he had a vision of the divine beauty of Bhagavan, it did not last. A divine voice declared, "You are not yet ready. This short vision was blessed because of your service to sadhus and to arouse in you a burning desire to see Me." The child spent the rest of his days chanting the divine names of the Lord and lovingly remembering His pastimes. When the time for his last breath came, his body fell, and the child was later reborn as Narada, the son of Lord Brahma.
week-6.Sage Vyasa's Samadhi Vision and Composin: In chapter 7, after Sage Narada left, Sage Vyasa sat in meditation. In the state of samadhi he saw all the divine pastimes of Bhagavan. Knowing that devotion to Krishna is the only easy means for the people of Kali Yuga to attain the ultimate good, he composed Srimad Bhagavatam - a scripture that would instill and inspire love for Bhagavan in the hearts of its listeners. He taught this to his son Sri Shuka who, though he was a self-realised soul always reveling in his own Self, was enamoured by the divine leelas and glories of Bhagavan.

week-7.Ashwatthama's Revenge and Arjuna Sparing: Suta Pauranika next started the story of Parikshith, which serves as a prelude to Krishna Katha - Srimad Bhagavatam begins where the Mahabharata ends. At the end of the Mahabharata war, Ashwatthama, the son of Dronacharya, sought to avenge the death of his father. Against the wish of even Duryodhana, he set out to kill the Pandavas in the middle of the night, but ended up killing their five sons instead - the Upapandavas. Waking to see the headless bodies of her five sons, Draupadi was inconsolable, and Arjuna vowed to bring her the head of the perpetrator. Frightened and cornered by Arjuna and Krishna, Ashwatthama in desperation hurled at them the powerful Brahmastra, which he did not know how to properly control or wield. Arjuna surrendered to the Lord, and Bhagavan instructed him to counter it with another Brahmastra and retract both of them. Arjuna did so, and then bound Ashwatthama. Lord Krishna tested Arjuna by asking him to kill Ashwatthama then and there, but knowing the heart of Krishna, Arjuna refrained from killing him and merely dragged the bound Ashwatthama to Draupadi's tent. Empathising with the pain of his mother Krupi, the compassionate Draupadi requested that he be released. Yudhishthira agreed, while Bhima countered it. Arjuna looked to Krishna again, and Bhagavan said, "Do that which would please all the parties and Me!" Arjuna insulted Ashwatthama by cutting off the gem in his head and then let him go.
week-7.Kunti's Stuti After Krishna Protects the: Krishna was set to depart from Hastinapura. While he was about to take leave of everyone, Uttara, the pregnant wife of Abhimanyu, came running to Krishna and surrendered. An insulted and angry Ashwatthama had hurled more Brahmastras to kill the child in her womb and all the Pandavas, and Bhagavan protected all of them. When Queen Kunti witnessed this, a beautiful soulful stuti, a song of praise, poured forth from her. Recognizing her nephew as the primal Lord of this universe, she glorified Lord Krishna in 26 verses. Kunti Devi listed all the times in her life when Bhagavan had protected her and her family, and said, "O Krishna! May such calamities befall me incessantly so that I would have your darshan always!" She prayed that her mind dwell constantly in Bhagavan and asked Him to stay longer in Hastinapura. Lord Krishna acquiesced and stayed back.
week-7.Bhishmacharya's Final Teachings and Bhis: King Yudhishthira refused to be crowned, as he felt guilty about the death of his kinsmen. To bring him clarity, Bhagavan Krishna took the Pandavas and Draupadi to the battlefield where Bhishmacharya lay on a bed of arrows. Bhishmacharya was moved to see them and recollected the hardships they had gone through. He instructed King Yudhishthira in all the dharmas and finally expanded the Bhagavata Dharma of Nama sankirtan in the form of the Vishnu Sahasranama. He then focused his mind on Bhagavan Sri Krishna alone and extolled Him in a beautiful stuti of 11 verses, praying in every verse for divine love. He recollected the special grace of Lord Krishna in the battlefield, where Bhagavan gave up His vow to not wield a weapon in order to uphold Bhishmacharya's vow to make Him wield one. Bhishmacharya finally remembered with great reverence the love that the Gopis of Vrindavan had for Lord Krishna, and gave up his mortal coil. Bhagavan then took leave of all at Hastinapuram and returned to Dwaraka.
week-7.Parikshith's Birth, Horoscope, and Namin: Sage Shaunaka asked Suta Pauranika about the story of Parikshith, who was saved by the Lord while in the womb of his mother, Uttara. As he was being scorched by the fire of Ashwatthama's Brahmastra, the baby in the womb beheld the wonderful form of the Lord in front of him, swirling His mace and quenching the fire. The child was then born to Uttara on an auspicious day, delighting everyone. When his horoscope was sketched, the brahmanas narrated the entire future of the child - that he would be a great king, that he would be cursed to die in seven days, and that he would ultimately attain Sri Krishna's lotus feet. Since he was protected and virtually 'given' by the Lord, he was called 'Vishnuraatha'; and because he kept searching for that wonderful form of the Lord that he had beheld while in his mother's womb, he was called Parikshith. Krishna came to Hastinapura for the Ashwamedha sacrifice conducted by Yudhishthira, and after completing three Ashwamedha sacrifices, Krishna returned to Dwaraka, with Arjuna accompanying him this time.
week-7.Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, and Vidura's De: Vidura returned to Hastinapura after ascertaining the truth about the Self from Sage Maitreya. Yudhishthira and his brothers were very happy to see him back, and Yudhishthira enquired about his travels and about the Yadavas. Vidura described everything in detail, leaving out the destruction of the Yadava kula, for he could not bring himself to break the bad news. Vidura waited for an opportune moment and counseled his brother Dhritarashtra, inspiring him to seek the ultimate truth about the Self. Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura then left Hastinapura without informing anyone. Finding them gone one morning, a pained Yudhishthira was consoled by Sage Narada, who told him they had gone to the ashram of sages in the southern Himalayas where Ganga Devi flows as seven streams, called Saptasrota; and that, having witnessed both Dhritarashtra and Gandhari give up their mortal coil, Vidura would go out again on a pilgrimage.
week-7.Arjuna's Realization and the End of the: Arjuna had gone to Dwaraka to see his relatives and had not returned even though many months had passed. Seeing ill omens everywhere, Yudhishthira began to worry and spoke of his apprehensions to Bhima. While he was conversing with Bhima, a dejected Arjuna returned, his face dark with sorrow. Arjuna broke down and revealed the fate of the Yadavas, who, while in an intoxicated state, fought among themselves, impelled by the curse of sages, and destroyed their own entire race. He recollected all the times Lord Krishna had been with the Pandavas, guiding and protecting them, and realized that all his prowess was Lord Krishna's grace and not his own. Kunti Devi gave up her body the moment she heard that Bhagavan had completed His leela on earth. Yudhishthira installed Parikshith as the king, and all the Pandavas, followed by Draupadi, left the kingdom, reached the Himalayas, and shed their bodies. Vidura too left his mortal coil in Prabhasa kshetra.
week-7.Parikshith's Vision of Dharma as a Bull: The noble king Parikshith ruled ably over the earth. He married King Uttara Kumara's daughter Iravati and begot four sons. Once, during his conquests, he beheld a strange divine vision. He saw a cow shedding tears profusely as it stood alongside a bull who was standing on only one leg, its other three legs having been broken. The bull was asking why the cow was in tears, and the cow revealed that it was because the Lord had left her. Parikshith then saw a man who looked like a rogue but was disguised as a king, hurting the cow and the bull. Parikshith angrily asked the man who he was, and asked the bull who had cut off his three legs. The bull did not point any fingers or blame the man, even though it was obvious that it was he who had hurt the bull. Parikshith then understood the bull to be Dharma, the cow to be Mother Earth, and the man posing as a king to be Kali Purusha. (When we gossip about the sinful activities of another, we get a portion of that sin; Dharma avoided that, and hence Parikshith could discern that the bull was Dharma.)
week-7.The Four Legs of Dharma: Tapas, Shaucham: The four legs of Dharma are: 1. Tapas - austerity; 2. Shaucham - purity; 3. Daya - compassion; 4. Satyam - truth. Except for satyam, all the other limbs of dharma (the bull) were broken. After subduing Kali Purusha, Parikshith restored the three broken legs of Dharma and continued to rule his kingdom well.
week-7.Parikshith Sparing Kali Purusha and the: When Parikshith was about to kill Kali Purusha, Kali Purusha fell at his feet and surrendered. Thus Parikshith refrained from killing him and provided him with four places to reside - gambling, alcohol, adultery, and violence (falsehood, intoxication, lust, and cruelty). When Kali Purusha requested one more place, Parikshith gave him 'gold' (rajoguna) as the fifth place to stay. Parikshith did not kill Kali Purusha and merely subdued him, even though this Kali was literally a storehouse of evils, because he knew that in the Kali yuga everyone could attain Bhagavan easily through the path of Namasankirtana. Another positive aspect of the age of Kali is that good intentions, even if not translated into action, are rewarded, while bad intentions are not punished until implemented through action. Like a bee, Parikshith discerned this nectar - the true essence - from the flower of Kaliyuga, and let it be.
